newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Tight window of opportunity for NZ easing - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Tight window of opportunity for NZ easing - analysts.

text.p: Any easing of monetary policy by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand looks set to be short-lived, analysts said on Tuesday in the light of a major speech by RBNZ Governor Don Brash.
Brash on Monday warned politicians they should defer next year's tax cuts unless they reined in spending plans.
The nationalist New Zealand First Party is in coalition talks with the conservative caretaker National Party government and centre-left Labour Party following an inconclusive election a month ago.

"I think the politicians will take on board what Brash said and do nothing about it," said one senior banker who declined to be named. "They have all got constituencies which they need to keep happy by spending more money."
"National need to do it because they want to be part of the government, and Labour and New Zealand First are both committed to spending more and running the surpluses down."

The banker said Brash was speaking under the mistaken premise the Reserve Bank Act would be left unchanged. At present the bank's sole focus is on price stability, defined as zero to two percent underlying inflation.

"At the very least the inflation target will be widened and, depending how desperate the other two are to form a government with NZ First, you could see other targets being added to the Reserve Bank Act and that will then give them scope to spend more," the banker said.
Banker Trust New Zealand Executive Vice President John McFarlane said the speech was a precursor to a relatively hawkish Monetary Policy Statement from the RBNZ on December 17.

"My expectation would be that they would potentially ease in the December Monetary policy Statement. Yesterday's speech did nothing for my confidence that that will in fact be the case -- or the window for easing could be relatively short," he said.
Westpac Bank Head of Financial Markets Chris Rand said he still expects an easing in December.

"The warning that he (Brash) was shooting across the bows was that if the government, of whatever persuasion it is when it is finally formed, starts to spend more, which will undoubtedly give impetus to the economy, then the easing could be very short-lived," Rand said.
"In a matter of months, and certainly the end of next year, people could be looking at higher rates again," he said.
Bank of New Zealand Treasury Economist Peter Jolly still sees an easing on the cards but agreed it may short-lived.
"They could ease and tighten back up when they find out the full extent of the fiscal programme in February," he said.
Brash said that tax reductions and expenditure increases announced in recent months amounted to a substantial turnaround in the fiscal position -- some four percent of GDP over two years.

He noted the currency had risen because of the attraction of high interest rates and suggested pressure on exporters could be reduced by ensuring the "overstretched" economy was not further stimulated by the next round of tax cuts.

Ironically, Brash's comments may end up boosting interest rates and the dollar further. He repeated the bank's often-stated view that a loosening of fiscal policy would require a monetary policy response.
McFarlane said that while the bank approved the $3 billion two-step tax cut package last year, it may be less sanguine now.

"Brash made it very clear what happens under that scenario -- interest rates stay high, the currency goes up and the adjustment is worn disproportionately by the export sector. That raises the risks that ultimately the economy hits the wall."

Currently BT and other private sector forecasters expect the economy to bottom out in the September quarter at about 1.7 percent annual growth and then, stimulated by the easing in December, the second round of tax cuts in July 1997 and the end of polical uncertainty, be boosted into another spurt of growth.
